title: Highly Selective and Active Cu-In2O3/C Nanocomposite for Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO2 to CO
abstract: The Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite was prepared by a simple solid-phase reduction method. The introduction of In2O3 into Cu/C to form the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite evidently enhances the electrocatalytic activity for the selective reduction of CO2 to CO. Specifically, the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite exhibits higher Faraday efficiency (FE=86.7%) at -0.48V vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO and larger current densities (55mA cm-2) under a low overpotential (-1.08V vs. RHE). These indicateits superior performance over many of the reported Cu-based catalysts[1-4]. It was also found that by rationally adjusting the applied potential, tunable syngas can be formed, which can be used to synthesize formic acid, methyl ether, methanol, synthetic fuels, or other bulk chemicals through appropriate industrial processes. Furthermore, the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite maintains good stability in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. This work demonstrates a novel strategy to convert CO2 into desired products with high energy efficiency and large current density under low overpotential by the rational designing of non-precious metal catalysts.

2 1.Introduction It is well known that the greenhouse effect, caused by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, and the energy crisis are two major problems troubling mankind. Therefore, the conversion of carbon dioxide into usable industrial chemicals has attracted widespread attention[5-10]. Conventional chemical methods for carbon dioxide reduction are not only costly but also environmentally hazardous. Currently, electrochemical CO2 reduction has aroused the interest of researchers all over the world, owing to its simple reaction process and controllable products[11-16]. Electrochemical CO2 reduction to valuable chemicals provides a promising pathway to the storage and utilization of renewable resources (generated from wind, solar, etc.). Electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide is a slow kinetic reaction, and its products in the aqueous solution of CO2 electrochemical reduction are complicated, primarily including HCOOH, CO, CH4, and C2H4[3, 7, 17-19]. In addition, the production of hydrogen is inevitable in electrochemical CO2 reduction. CO is the basic material for synthesizing carbonaceous fuels and large-scale chemicals. Therefore, the development and application of catalysts with high activity and selectivity for CO is a key factor in electrocatalyzing CO2 reduction. Currently, various electrocatalysts, including metal catalysts (such as Au, Ag, Pd, and Cu)[20-23], non-metal catalysts (such as N-doped carbon nanotubes, and covalent organic framework)[24-26], and molecular catalysts (such as cobalt phthalocyanine)[27-29]. have been widely used in electrochemical CO2 reduction. Among these catalysts, copper-based catalysts have unique catalytic capabilities for converting CO2 into various hydrocarbons[19]. However, most copper-based electrocatalysts currently have problems such as high potential, poor selectivity, and poor catalytic stability. To overcome these, a second component is introduced to improve the selectivity of the product. For example, Cu-Pd alloy catalysts with various compositions can adjust the selectivity of Cu catalysts in electrochemical CO2 reduction[30].The Faraday efficiency of Cu-Pd alloy nanoparticles (NPs) (87% at -0.9 V vs. RHE) is significantly higher than that of Cu NPs in the reduction of CO2 to CO. However, Pd is a noble metal that is too costly to be used in large-scale production. Therefore, non-precious metal catalysts need to be developed to make commercially viable catalysts. Recently, copper nanoparticles dispersed on carbon aerogels were
3 reported to exhibit a Faraday efficiency of 75.6% in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO under a low overpotential (-0.49 V)[2]. Indium was introduced into copper-based catalysts to improve their catalytic performance, which proved conducive to electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO at mild overpotentials [31]. It was also reported that CO2 can be converted to syngas and formate on Cu-In alloy, but the Faraday efficiency for CO formation and the partial current density (< 1 mA/cm2 at -1.0 V vs. RHE) need to be further improved[3, 4]. In this work, a noble metal-free Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite was synthesize by a simple solid-phase reduction method. By introducing the In2O3 component into Cu/C, the electrocatalytic activity of the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite for the selective reduction of CO2 to CO was significantly improved. It is interesting to note that the proportions of CO/H2 can be adjusted from 1/1 to 1/3 in the range of -0.68 V to -0.48 V vs. RHE, which can be used to synthesize bulk chemicals and fuels through appropriate industrial processes.

sections.heading: 2. 1 Materials
sections.text: Carbon black (VulcanXC-72R, ~250 m2 g-1) was purchased from Cabot Corporation (USA). Cu(NO3)2·3H2O (≥99.0%), In(NO3)3·4.5H2O (≥99.5%), KHCO3 (≥99.5%), Na2SO4 (≥99.0%), and C2H5OH (≥99.7%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). D2O (99.9%), HCOOH (>99%), andC2H6OS (≥99.95%) were purchased from Aladdin Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Nafion117 solution (5%)was purchased from Aldrich Chemical Co., Inc. (USA). Ultrapure deionized water (≥18.2 MΩ cm) was used to prepare the solutions.

sections.heading: 2.2 Synthesis of Cu-In2O3/Cnanocomposite
sections.text:
Carbon black (50 mg, VulcanXC-72R) was dispersed in 30 mL of deionized water by ultrasonic processing for 30 min. In addition, 191 mg of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O and 332.6 mg of In(NO3)3·4.5H2O were dispersed in 10 mL of deionized water, stirred for 10 min to completely dissolve, and mixed with the carbon black dispersion and sonicated for 40 min. After sonication, a black suspension was obtained, which was concentrated to 2–5 mL in a 60 °C water bath and put into a square porcelain boat. After drying, it was placed in a high-temperature tube furnace for calcination at 500 °C with a temperature increase rate of 5 °C min-1 in a 5% H2/Ar atmosphere, maintained at
4 500 °C for 2 h, then cooled to 25 °C at a rate of 5 °C min-1. After that, the solid product was centrifuged, washed with deionized water. Then it was dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 48 h. For comparison, Cu/C and In2O3/C were synthesized by the same method as described above without In(NO3)3·4.5H2O or Cu(NO3)2·3H2O.

sections.heading: 2.3 Characterization of the as-prepared composites
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra were recorded using a PANalyticalX’Pert Pro diffractometer. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra were obtained using a VG ESCALAB250 multitechnique X-ray photoelectron spectrometer. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were taken with a JEOL JSM-7500F field emission scanning electron microscope. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a Talos F2100X transmission electron microscope, and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images were obtained using an FEI Tecnai GE transmission electron microscope. Electrocatalytic tests were performed in an electrochemical workstation (CHI 650E, Chen Hua Instruments Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China).

sections.heading: 2.4 Electrochemistry Test
sections.text:
The test for electrocatalytic properties was performed in an electrochemical cell with a two-chamber and three-electrode configuration. The electrolyte was 0.5 M KHCO3 saturated with carbon dioxide. A Pt electrode and Ag/AgCl electrode were used as the counter electrode and reference, respectively. The working electrode was prepared by dropping 60 μL of the catalyst dispersion on carbon paper (1 cm × 3 cm). Specifically, 5 mg of the catalyst was dispersed in a solution of 900 μL ethanol and 100 μL of a 5% Nafion 117 solution. A homogeneous dispersion was obtained after sonication for 1 h. The working and reference electrodes were placed in the cathode compartment and the counter electrode was placed in the anode compartment. The anode and cathode compartments were separated by a Nafion 117 ion exchange membrane. Before the test, high-purity carbon dioxide was introduced into the cathode chamber at a flow rate of 30 mL min-1 for 1 h. Linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) was performed in a KHCO3 solution saturated with CO2 or N2 at a scan rate of 10 mV s-1. The timing current curve (IT) was tested in a KHCO3 solution saturated with CO2 at a constant potential, and constant magnetic stirring was maintained
5 during the test process. The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was calculated using the electric double-layer method. The roughness was calculated using the electric double-layer capacitance of the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve. The calculation formula for ECSA is as follows [32]: ECSA = Rf ×S, (1) where S is the actual surface area of the catalyst, which is usually equal to the area of the catalyst supported on the carbon paper (S = 1 cm-2). Rf is the roughness factor, given by the following: Rf = Cdl / Z, (2) where Cdl is the electric double-layer capacitance and Z is a constant. The CV curves under a series of different scanning rates (10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 mV s-1) were measured by cyclic voltammetry at -0.3 V to -0.1 V vs. saturated calomel electrode (SCE). The scanning rates were plotted against the corresponding current at -0.2 V vs. SCE to obtain a straight line, and the straight-line slope yields the electric double-layer capacitance. Electrochemical impedance (EIS) was measured in a 0.2 M Na2SO4 solution with a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz at 1.28 V vs. SCE. Because the catalyst was completed on the same working electrode, the roughness factor Rf usedin the formula is the same by default; therefore, only the electrochemically active surface area needs to be considered when comparing the Cdl value.

sections.heading: 2.5 Measurement of reduction products
sections.text:
The liquid product was analyzed qualitatively and quantitatively by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR). The specific operation is as follows: 0.5 mL of catholytewas mixed with 0.1 mL of D2O and 5 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) solution, with the DMSO used as an internal standard. Qualitative and quantitative analyses were performed accordingly. The formula for calculating the Faraday efficiency (FE) for formic acid production is as follows: FE = 2ntotalF/Q, where 2 denotes the number of electrons transferred when formic acid is produced, ntotal indicates the total amount of formic acid, which is derived from the quantitative analysis results of NMR, F is the Faraday constant, 96485 C mol-1, and Q is the total charge transferred in the reaction system [33, 34]. All potentials were converted into a RHE potential using the formula: ERHE = ESCE + 0.059 × pH + EθSCE (EθSCE = 0.241 V vs. normal hydrogen electrode (NHE) at 25 ℃) [35, 36].

sections.heading: 3.1 Characterization of Cu-In2O3 /C nanocomposite
sections.text:
The XRD spectra of Cu-In2O3/C, Cu/C, and In2O3/C are shown in Fig. 1. From Fig. 1 curves (a) and (b), it can be observed that the diffraction peaks at 43.3° and 50.4° correspond to the (111) and (200) crystalline faces of face-centered cubic (fcc) Cu in Cu-In2O3/C and Cu/C (JCPDF No. 04-0836). In Fig. 1 curve (a), the diffraction peak at approximately 36.4° is attributed to the characteristic peak of Cu2O, indicating the existence of Cu2O in Cu/C (JCPDF No. 05-0667). As shown in Fig. 1 curves (b) and (c), the diffraction peaks at 21.5°, 30.5°, 35.4°, 51.0°, and 60.6°are assigned to the crystalline faces of (211), (222), (400), (440), and (622) of In2O3 (JCPDF No. 06-0416), respectively.
Fig. 1. XRD patterns: (a) Cu/C, (b) Cu-In2O3/C, and (c) In2O3/C.
The valence states of copper and indium were determined by XPS. The fitting method of XPS peaks is described in the supplementary material. As indicated in Fig. 2A, there are two strong peaks at 444.9 eV and 452.5 eV for Cu-In2O3/C, and two peaks at 445.1 eV and 452.7 eV for In2O3/C, which are, respectively, assigned to In3d5/2 and In3d3/2 binding energies, indicating the presence of a positive trivalent cation of In and further proving the existence of In2O3[3]. As displayed in Fig. 2B and C, two Cu 2p characteristic peaks ascribed to Cu (0) are found at 932.8 eV & 953.0 eV for Cu-In2O3/C and 932.7 eV & 953.0 eV for Cu/C[3]. According to the reported binding energy of Cu2O[37, 38], a small amount of Cu2O is present in Cu-In2O3/C and Cu/C. This result is consistent with the XRD analysis. The XPS spectra of C1s in Cu-In2O3/C are shown in
7
Fig. 2D. The characteristic peak at 284.5 eV is ascribed to the C1s binding energy[39].
Fig. 2. (A) In3d profile of (a) Cu-In2O3/C and (b) In2O3/C. (B) Cu 2p XPS profile of Cu-In2O3/C. (C) Cu 2p XPS profile of Cu/C. (D) C1s XPS profile of Cu-In2O3/C.
The SEM images of Cu-In2O3/C, Cu/C and In2O3/C composites are shown in Fig. S1. It can be observed that all the nano-sized Cu-In2O3/C, Cu/C and In2O3/C composites are uniformly distributed. The TEM and HRTEM images of Cu-In2O3/C, Cu/C, and In2O3/C are shown in Fig. 3. From the HRTEM image of Cu-In2O3/C (Fig. 3C), a lattice fringe spacing of 0.292 nm is observed, which is attributed to the (222) crystal plane of fcc In2O3[40]. The lattice fringes assigned to Cu are not found, which may be because the amount of metallic Cu in the selected HRTEM region is below the test limit. However, the presence of Cu can be clearly confirmed through the analysis of the element mapping images below (Fig. 4C). Correspondingly, a lattice fringe spacing of 0.292 nm was also observed in the HRTEM images of In2O3/C (Fig. 3G). In addition, lattice fringes of 0.208 nm can be observed in the HRTEM images of Cu/C (Fig. 3E), which belongs to the (111) crystal plane of fcc Cu[3]. High-angle annular dark field-scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and element map analysis were performed to further confirm the morphology of Cu-In2O3/C. As shown in Fig. 4B–E, it can be observed that Cu and In atoms are evenly distributed on the carbon support. Scanning the profile of Cu and In
8
elements in Cu-In2O3/C (Fig. 4A) along the corresponding cross-sectional line further confirms that Cu and In2O3 coexist in the composites (Fig. 4F).
Fig. 3. TEM images: (A–C) Cu-In2O3/C, (D–E) Cu/C, and (F–G) In2O3/C.
Fig. 4. (A) HAADF-STEM images of Cu-In2O3/C. Elemental mapping images of Cu-In2O3/C of (B) C, (C) Cu, (D) O, and (E) In. (F) The distribution of Cu and In elements along the corresponding cross-sectional line shown in (A). 3.2 Electrocatalytic performance of Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite
LSV measurements were used to study the catalytic performance of the composite for the reduction of CO2. The LSV curve was tested in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution at a potential range of -0.067 to -1.166 V vs. RHE and a sweep speed of 10 mV s-1. As shown in Fig. 5B and C, the initial potential and current density of the LSV for Cu/C and In2O3/C are not
9
significantly different between the CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution and the N2-saturated KHCO3 solution. However, when Cu-In2O3/C is used as an electrocatalyst, the initial potential and current density in a CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution are much larger than those in a N2-saturated KHCO3 solution (Fig. 5A), and a higher current density and lower overpotentialas compared with those of Cu/C and In 2 O 3 /C are observed (Fig. 5D), which indicates that the combination of Cu and In2O3 is conducive to enhancing the electrocatalytic activity for the reduction of CO2.

Gas chromatogram (GC) and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) of the gas phase and liquid phase products are provided in the supplementary material (Fig. S2-S5).The Faraday efficiency graphs of electrochemical CO2 reduction on Cu-In2O3/C, Cu/C, and In2O3/C composites at different potentials are shown in Fig. 6A–C. As shown in Fig. 6B, the primary product is H2 on Cu/C, which indicates that the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) reaction preferentially occurs in the aqueous electrolyte Cu/C. By introducing In2O3, the primary product becomes CO at -0.48 V vs. RHE (Fig. 6A), and the Faraday efficiency of Cu-In2O3/C for CO2 reduction to CO can reach
10
86.7%, which is much larger than that of Cu/C (FECO=13%) and In2O3 (FECO=41%). This indicates that the selective reduction of CO2 to CO is greatly improved by combining In2O3 with Cu. The primary product of the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction of In2O3 /C is HCOOH at -0.98 V vs. RHE (Fig. 6C). For CO2 reduction to HCOOH, the Faraday efficiency of In2O3/C was 64% at -0.98 V vs. RHE, and the current density was 10 mA cm-2. It indicates that the catalytic selectivity can be controlled by adjusting the component of the catalyst.

Current density is a key parameter for evaluating the catalytic performance of catalysts. Under the premise of maintaining a high current density, reducing the electrocatalytic overpotential is key to achieving high energy efficiency. As shown in Fig. 7A, the total current density of Cu-In2O3/C has the largest value at each potential, reaching 55 mA cm-2 at -1.08 V vs. RHE, which shows that the synergies of Cu and In2O3 can enhance the electrocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction. In the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to form syngas, CO, and HCOOH, the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite as an electrocatalyst also has the largest current density as compared with Cu/C and In2O3/C (Fig. 7B–D). Moreover, it is also found that the ratio of syngas products on Cu-In2O3/C at -0.68 V, -0.58 V, and -0.48 V vs. RHE are close to the ideal ratio of synthetic aldehyde (H2:CO=1:1), Fischer–Tropschsynthesis (H2:CO=1:2), and syngas fermentation (H2:CO=1:3), respectively. This reveals that the tunable syngas composition can be obtained by rationally controlling the applied potential.

To study the effect of the ECSA on catalytic performance, the CV curves under a series of different scanning rates (10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 mV s-1) were measured by cyclic voltammetry at -0.3 V to -0.1 V vs. SCE (Fig. 8A–C). The scanning rates were plotted against the corresponding current at -0.2 V vs. SCE to obtain a straight line, and the straight-line slope yields the electric double-layer capacitance (Fig. 8A–C).According to the formulae given in Eq. 1 and 2[32], the Cdl values of Cu-In2O3/C are 5.807 mF cm-2, which are approximately twice and 4.2 times larger than those of Cu/C (2.979 mF cm-2) and In2O3/C (1.372 mF cm-2), respectively. This indicates that the ECSA of Cu-In2O3/C is much larger than that of Cu/C and In2O3/C. A larger ECSA will provide more active sites, which helps to enhance the electrocatalytic activity for the reduction of CO2, increasing the current density at a lower overpotential.
12
In addition, continuous CO2 reduction was performed at -0.48 V vs. RHE for 4 h to evaluate the catalytic stability of Cu-In2O3/C. The liquid-phase products were analyzed every half an hour during the test. The experimental results (Fig. 9) reveal that the Faraday efficiency and the current density of CO remain almost unchanged during the test. The Faraday efficiency for CO2 reduction to CO is approximately 84% with Cu-In2O3/C (Fig. 9A), indicating the good stability of Cu-In2O3/C in electrochemical CO2 reduction. Correspondingly, the same test was performed at -0.98 V vs. RHE for 4 h with In2O3/C. It is found that the current density first decreases and then tends to be stable at approximately 12.5 mA cm-2 after 1 h, and the Faraday efficiency is above 60% (Fig. 9B).
13
To further study the charge transfer kinetics of the catalyst in electrochemical CO2 reduction of, the electrochemical impedance test was performed in a 0.2 M Na2SO4 solution. The AC impedance diagram under the open-circuit voltage is shown in Fig. 10. The high-frequency region is related to the process of the electrode reaction, namely the charge transfer process. The diameter of the high-frequency semicircle is equal to the charge transfer resistance (Rct), and the low-frequency region is related to the diffusion process of the reactants or products. The Nyquist impedance data can be analyzed by fitting an equivalent circuit.

It can be observed from Table 1 that the Rct value calculated by fitting is 273.63 Ω for Cu-In2O3/C, which is significantly smaller than that for Cu/C (461.67 Ω) and In2O3/C (654.93 Ω). sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
The Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite was synthesized by a simple solid-phase reduction method in a mixed hydrogen and argon atmosphere. The as-prepared Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite is highly selective and active in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO, with a Faraday efficiency of 86.7% at -0.48 V vs. RHE and a large current density of 55 mA cm-2 at a low overpotential of -1.08 V vs. RHE, which indicateits superior performance over several reported Cu-based catalysts. Moreover, the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite shows excellent durability which can be testified by almost no attenuation of the Faraday efficiency and the current density for 4 h in electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. The catalytic activity and selectivity are correlated with the adsorption ability of the corresponding intermediates and the desorption ability of products on catalysts. It can be proposed that the introduction of In2O3 is correlated with the enhanced adsorption ability of the obtained Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite for the *COOH intermediate and the desorption ability of *CO at lower overpotentials, which favors the selectivereduction of CO2 to CO[3, 4, 41, 42].
Moreover, the proportions of CO/H2 can be adjusted by rationally controlling the applied potential to obtain tunable syngas which can be used for large-scale production of valuable industrial chemicals through appropriate industrial processes. In a comprehensive evaluation of energy efficiency and economic feasibility, the Cu-In2O3/C nanocomposite is highly advantageous over several noble metal catalysts [19, 43, 44]. The study will provide new insights into the design and utilization of non-precious metal catalysts for the highly active and selective electrochemical reduction of CO2. Acknowledgements
